titulo.texto: Six and Seven Halls: Flora, Fauna, and Agriculture

frase_gancho.texto: Chalchiuhtlicue, Chicomecóatl, Xipe Tótec, and the models of a chinampa and a market.

puente_narrativo.texto: Enter the Eight Hall, the last one, where the story moves from the Mexica to the colonial city.

guion_corto.texto: The Six and Seven Halls show the natural and agricultural world. The Six Hall, on flora and fauna, includes images of Chalchiuhtlicue, Chicomecóatl, and Xipe Tótec, gods related to water, maize, and renewal. The Seven Hall, on agriculture, shows crops, a model of a chinampa, and another of the Tlatelolco market. These halls shift the focus from the great rituals to daily life: what people grew, what they ate, and how the market was organized. They help us understand the foundation of the city's economy, and they bring closer a culture that is sometimes imagined only through its rituals.

guion_largo.texto:
After the halls of the two great gods, the tour moves down in scale. The Six and Seven Halls deal with nature and the countryside, that is, with what sustained life in the city.

The Six Hall is about flora and fauna. In it appear images of three important figures: Chalchiuhtlicue, Chicomecóatl, and Xipe Tótec. Chalchiuhtlicue is associated with the waters, Chicomecóatl with maize and sustenance, and Xipe Tótec with the renewal of vegetation. Specialists may nuance these associations, but it is clear that these are gods related to natural life, to plants, and to the cycles of the year.

Think about how this theme connects with what you saw earlier. The Tláloc side of the temple was dedicated to water and fertility. These figures are, in a way, relatives of that world: they show different faces of the same thing, the earth, the water, and the cycle of plants.

The Seven Hall, on agriculture, shows crops and two models. One represents a chinampa, which is a farming plot built on the water. Chinampas were a form of agriculture typical of the Basin of Mexico, and they helped feed the city. The other model represents the Tlatelolco market, the great market. Seeing them helps you imagine what daily life was like around the temple.

These models have a special value. The remains of the temple show the ritual side of the city, but they don't say much about what happened in the streets and the canals. A model lets you imagine the movement, the goods, and the people, and that complements what you learn in the earlier halls. It is a good moment to rest your eyes from the stone pieces and look at whole scenes.

If you are short on time, these are the halls that can be seen most quickly. But if you are interested in the daily life of the Mexica, they deserve a pause. Notice the crops on display: they are the basis of the diet and of the economy. Without them, there would have been neither empire nor temple. That is the idea that ties together everything you have seen in the museum.

You can also compare the open-air market with the markets you know. Some markets in Mexico City are still very lively places of exchange, and the idea of the open-air market is part of that heritage. It is a way to connect what you see in the museum with the city of today, and to see that some customs have very deep roots.

The last hall awaits you with a change of era. Take a breath before going in, because the tone changes a great deal. We will move from the Mexica to the conquest and to what came after.

texto: Look for the images of Chalchiuhtlicue, Chicomecóatl, and Xipe Tótec
Observe the model of the chinampa and how the cultivation is organized
Compare the Tlatelolco market with a present-day market

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Templo Mayor only held objects of war and sacrifice.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Its halls also show flora, fauna, crops, a chinampa, and the Tlatelolco market.
